meta.question: We are considering allowing students to use generative AI coding assistants in the first-year C programming course. Will it actually improve learning outcomes? How should it be introduced?

research_frame.question: We are considering allowing students to use generative AI coding assistants in the first-year C programming course. Will it actually improve learning outcomes? How should it be introduced?

learner.prior_knowledge: The vast majority are absolute beginners with no prior programming experience or only minimal self-study; they are unfamiliar with C syntax, compile errors, and the debugging workflow; their high-school mathematics foundation is average and logical thinking is still being trained.
learner.special_characteristics: Motivation and self-discipline vary widely; curiosity about and receptiveness to AI tools are high; students easily treat AI answers as final results without understanding them; some students have limited English proficiency and struggle with English error messages and documentation; the unified final exam is a hard assessment constraint.

course.subject: C_programming
course.duration: One semester (about 16 weeks), with 2 credit hours of theory + 2 hours of lab per week, and a unified machine-based and written final exam.

intervention.ai_tool: Mainstream generative AI coding assistants (e.g., GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT/Claude code generation, Cursor, etc.), based on the tools students can actually access; no single brand is mandated.
intervention.allowed_usage: Pilot scheme: allowed for debugging errors, explaining concepts, code walkthroughs, and refactoring suggestions; submitting AI-generated code directly as homework answers is prohibited; lab sessions include independent assessment segments without AI.
intervention.frequency: On-demand use during weekly lab sessions; restricted use during homework phases; usage count and scenarios recorded via logs or self-report.
intervention.duration: Co-extensive with the course for 16 weeks, covering the entire semester, with end-of-term assessment comparison.

research_frame.comparison: Randomized controlled or quasi-experimental design: parallel classes in the same major / random groups within the same class. Treatment group: allowed to use AI coding assistants under guided rules; control group: traditional teaching with AI prohibited. Both groups keep identical content, workload, and instructor effort, and are compared only on the same unified machine-based and written final exam; the same machine-based exam is administered as a pre-test at the start of the term to control baseline differences.

scope.time_range: First semester of academic year 2025-2026 (16-week teaching cycle)
scope.geography: Regular undergraduate universities in mainland China (pilot targeting first-year Computer Science majors at our university)

inclusion_criteria: First-year freshmen majoring in Computer Science and Technology at our university
Taking the C Programming course for the first time this semester
Able to participate in the entire experiment and accept random assignment
Consent to AI usage logging and participation in end-of-term assessments
exclusion_criteria: Students with systematic programming experience before enrollment or prior programming competition participation
Students who have already completed C or an equivalent course
Students unable to complete the full course (leave of absence, major transfer, course withdrawal)
Students who decline random assignment or usage logging
research_frame.success_condition: If the treatment group's independent programming scores on the end-of-term unified machine-based and written exams are not significantly lower than the control group (non-inferiority), and AI usage frequency is positively correlated with score gains, and dependency risk indicators (independent task completion rate without AI) do not significantly worsen, then introducing AI coding assistants can be judged net beneficial, forming generalizable introduction rules and accompanying instructional design; otherwise the policy is tightened or revoked.

decision.decision_question: Should first-year university C programming students be allowed to use generative AI coding assistants? Will it actually improve learning outcomes? How should it be introduced?
decision.target_population: Zero-baseline freshmen majoring in Computer Science and Technology at regular undergraduate universities in mainland China (taking C Programming for the first time, with no systematic programming experience, wide variation in motivation and self-discipline, and the unified machine-based and written final exams as hard assessment constraints).
decision.target_context: A one-semester ~16-week compulsory core course with 2 credit hours of theory + 2 hours of lab per week; the pilot intervention allows students to use mainstream GenAI coding assistants (Copilot, ChatGPT/Claude code generation, Cursor, etc.) under guided rules, prohibits submitting AI-generated code directly as homework answers, and includes independent no-AI assessment segments in lab sessions; success requires the treatment group to be non-inferior to the control group on the end-of-term no-AI unified machine-based and written exams, with no significant worsening of dependency risk indicators.
supported_claims: Unrestrained, unfettered use of AI (a standard ChatGPT-like interface where answers can be copied directly) significantly harms independent exam performance after AI removal: in Bastani's three-arm RCT, the GPT Base group scored 17% lower on independent exams than the control group that never used AI (statistically significant, PNAS 2025, quality score 9); the mechanism is that students use GPT as a crutch and copy answers directly (only 51% correct answers, 42% of which were logic errors) while self-assessment is overly optimistic and students do not notice the learning impairment (E-002)

Well-designed guardrails can combine practice performance gains with independent-exam safety: in the same RCT, the guardrailed GPT Tutor (teacher-designed prompts, no direct answers) improved practice scores by 127%, and the negative effect on independent exams after AI removal was essentially eliminated (-0.004, not significant) (E-003)

Task performance gains with AI present are supported by multiple studies: Bastani practice scores +48% (no guardrails) / +127% (guardrails) (E-001); Kazemitabaar's 10-17-year-old programming novices using Codex improved completion rates 1.15x and scores 1.8x (E-004); Shihab's undergraduates using Copilot completed brownfield tasks 35% faster, made 50% more progress, and spent 11% less time writing code by hand (E-011, E-012) — but these are all task performance under AI-accessible conditions and do not constitute evidence of learning outcomes

AI-assisted training does not necessarily translate into learning retention without AI: Kazemitabaar learners who used Codex during training showed no significant difference from the control group on a one-week delayed post-test (null) (E-005)

Novices (structurally similar to the target population) show amplified illusions of competence and metacognitive difficulties under GenAI assistance: Prather's 21 lab sessions show students believing they performed better than they actually did, with cognitive dissonance (E-008)
GenAI benefits are highly differentiated: accelerators benefit while strugglers keep struggling, and the gap between novices and stronger students widens (E-009)
Students using AI worry that they do not understand how AI suggestions work and call for pedagogical designs that promote reflection on the principles behind suggestions (E-013)

A qualitative case study (n=3, EFL writing) shows students both value AI's assistance (reducing uncertainty, clarifying concepts, providing feedback) and worry about over-reliance and academic authenticity (E-006, E-007) — used only as pedagogical design cues, not quantitative policy evidence

High-quality counter-evidence exists in the evidence set and has not been discarded (skeptic negative_results_dropped risk: low): E-002's -17% and E-003's guardrail-eliminated negative effect stand side by side, and E-005's null result is faithfully recorded

The challenge AI poses to introductory programming assessment (current AI can solve a substantial share of typical introductory problems) stands as background, but the Denny review item (E-010) is only abstract-verified with status UNSUPPORTED and cannot be used as quantitative evidence
uncertain_claims: Whether guardrails can reproduce the 'both/and' effect in the C introductory context: E-003's guardrail effect was only validated in a single context (high-school mathematics with teacher-designed prompts), prompt quality and guardrail effect are confounded in the design, and replicability was not separately tested

Sustained effects over a full 16-week semester: all intervention windows are shorter or much shorter than a semester (Bastani: only 4 in-class 90-minute sessions; Kazemitabaar: short training period plus one-week post-test; Shihab: single lab session), novelty effects cannot be excluded, and there is no evidence on long-term engagement or maintenance of learning effects

Semester-level retention and cross-course transfer (e.g., data structures): only Kazemitabaar provides a one-week delayed post-test (null); Bastani's independent exam is an immediate measurement after AI removal (near transfer); there is no evidence across task types or courses
Control-group compliance: no study verifies whether control participants actually refrained from using AI; policy contamination risk is untested and may affect effect-size estimates

Tool-generation extrapolation: evidence is based on 2023-2025 Codex/GPT-3.5-4 generation tools; students in the pilot year face GPT-5-class models and deeply IDE-integrated agents, where benefits and dependency risks may both amplify, so effect sizes cannot be directly extrapolated
Novelty-effect component in positive effects: engagement and score gains under short interventions may be inflated, and whether they survive after novelty fades is uncertain

Robustness of small-sample positive effects: Shihab's p<0.05 effects at n=10 (within-subject design compounded by order/learning effects) and Marzuki's n=3 qualitative themes are fragile and cannot serve as policy basis

The task type in Shihab's undergraduate sample (brownfield legacy web codebase) does not match first-year C introductory tasks, and the transferability of its 35%/50% effects to the C introductory context is uncertain
Wermelinger's assessment-distortion argument (Copilot 16/24 introductory problems) is only FETCH_PARTIAL verified (institutional repository abstract page) and lacks full-text-level verification
contradicted_claims: 'Allowing students to ask AI directly for answers (unguardrailed use) improves learning' — directly refuted by E-002: the unguardrailed GPT Base group scored significantly 17% lower on no-AI independent exams

'AI-present task performance gains equal learning gains' — refuted by E-002/E-005: E-001's +48%/+127% practice gains coexist with the same study's E-002 -17% independent-exam harm; E-005's retention post-test is null; the higher-validity measurements (no-AI independent exams, delayed post-tests) are precisely the ones yielding negative or null results
'Students can accurately perceive AI's impact on their learning' — refuted by E-002 (overly optimistic self-assessment, failure to notice learning impairment) and E-008 (illusion of competence)
'AI assistance benefits all novices uniformly' — refuted by E-009: benefits are highly differentiated, strugglers keep struggling, and the gap between strong and weak students widens
what_can_be_claimed: The impact of allowing AI on learning outcomes depends entirely on usage-rule design: unguardrailed use causes empirically demonstrated independent-exam harm (E-002, high-quality RCT), while guardrailed use eliminates that negative effect (E-003) — this is the most reliable, decision-relevant policy conclusion in this evidence set

AI-present task performance (practice scores, completion rates, scores, speed, progress) improves across studies (E-001, E-004, E-011, E-012), but this only supports 'AI helps students complete tasks while present', not 'AI improves learning outcomes'
Independent-exam harm from unguardrailed use is an empirical risk rather than a theoretical concern, and directly threatens any 'copy answers freely' policy in the first-year C course (E-002)

Novice students face risks of illusion of competence, amplified metacognitive difficulties, and differentiated benefits when using GenAI; zero-baseline first-year freshmen are a high-incidence group for strugglers, requiring metacognitive training and failure detection (E-008, E-009)
There is currently no evidence that AI assistance improves learning retention (delayed post-test) (E-005 null), and semester-level retention is entirely blank
No controlled causal evidence exists for first-year zero-baseline C freshmen over a full semester; any policy decision is made on an evidence gap — the pilot itself fills that gap

The pilot should use no-AI independent assessment as the sole learning-outcome criterion; task performance metrics (homework completion rate, speed) may only be reported separately as process indicators (consistent with the measurement direction of E-002/E-003/E-005)
what_cannot_be_claimed: Cannot claim that 'allowing first-year freshmen to use GenAI coding assistants will improve C learning outcomes' — no study directly covers this population and context; the population-closest study (Shihab n=10) is underpowered and mismatched in task type, and all learning measurements (independent exams, delayed post-tests) are negative or null

Cannot use E-001's +48%/+127% practice scores, E-004's 1.15x/1.8x completion and scores, or E-011/E-012's 35% faster/50% more progress as evidence of 'learning gains' — all are AI-present task performance where AI can directly produce results, and 'learned' cannot be distinguished from 'copied'
Cannot claim unguardrailed use is safe — E-002 clearly shows a significant -17% negative effect
Cannot claim the guardrail scheme necessarily works in the C context — E-003 was only validated in a single context (high-school mathematics with teacher-designed prompts)
Cannot use E-010 (Denny review, UNSUPPORTED) to claim 'homework assessment is completely broken and must be fully redesigned' — this item is only abstract-verified and the full text was not retrieved
Cannot use E-006 (n=3 EFL writing qualitative) or E-011/E-012 (n=10 brownfield tasks) as quantitative basis for 'AI introduction is net beneficial'
Cannot directly extrapolate effect sizes from 2023-2025 tools to the 2026 GPT-5-class agent environment
Cannot claim semester-level retention or cross-course transfer (e.g., performance in data structures) — no corresponding evidence exists
missing_evidence: A controlled study of zero-baseline first-year C freshmen over a full 16-week semester (current evidence requires extrapolation across two dimensions — high school → university and math/web → C introductory — with high external-validity risk)
Direct validation of guardrail effects in the C introductory context (replicating E-003's design: unguardrailed / guardrailed / control three arms with no-AI independent assessment)
Semester-level retention measurement (delayed retest 2-4 weeks after term end) and cross-course transfer tracking (subsequent data structures course performance)
Control-group compliance verification (contamination check of whether controls actually refrained from AI) and intention-to-treat analysis
Instructor/TA effect control and guardrail replicability verification (across ≥2 teachers or classes) — E-003's guardrail effect is confounded with teacher prompt quality
Systematic no-AI independent post-tests in the Shihab/Kazemitabaar contexts (E-004 only has a one-week post-test that is null; E-011/E-012 have no no-AI post-test at all)
Effect data for current-generation (GPT-5-class) tools in introductory programming education (tool-generation drift)
Stratified effect data for zero-baseline novices: evidence on whether differentiated interventions for strugglers (metacognitive training, failure detection) work
Full-text-level verification of Wermelinger's assessment-distortion claim (currently FETCH_PARTIAL, institutional repository abstract only)
Sample-size design supported by a power analysis referencing Bastani's -17% effect size (avoiding n=10-class samples)
decision.decision_rationale: The evidence does not allow directly adopting (ADOPT) the 'allow use' policy: all positive effects (E-001/E-004/E-011/E-012) are task performance with AI present, while the highest-validity learning measurements give negative or null results (E-002: -17% significant on the no-guardrail independent exam; E-005: null retention), and no study directly covers the target context of 'first-year zero-baseline C freshmen + full semester' (skeptic overall_risk=high, methodology CONCERN). But the evidence equally does not support direct rejection (REJECT): E-003 shows that guardrailed AI (teacher-designed prompts, no direct answers) can eliminate the independent-exam negative effect while greatly improving practice scores, showing that the benefits and risks of 'allowing use' depend entirely on usage-rule design; tools are already widespread and their capabilities keep growing, so the practical feasibility of an outright ban is doubtful. Under this tension, pilot is the only evidence-supported path forward: use the randomized controlled (or quasi-experimental) pilot already designed in the frame to directly test whether E-003's guardrail conditions hold in the target context, set the end-of-term no-AI unified machine-based and written exams as the sole learning-outcome criterion (matching E-002/E-003's measurement approach), use non-inferiority as the success condition, and set a mid-term stop point (tighten the policy if the mid-term no-AI independent quiz shows a significant negative effect). The pilot is not 'waiting and watching'; it is the most direct way to fill the evidence gap (population_external_validity: high) and the guardrail extrapolation risk (E-003 single context), and E-002's -17% effect size can inform a power analysis for the sample size.
decision.reason_for_disagreement: This adjudication clearly disagrees with three alternative positions: (1) Disagreement with direct ADOPT — the E-001 +127% and E-011 35% faster figures cited by those who claim 'allowing use is net beneficial' are all AI-present task performance; within the same study, E-002's -17% independent-exam harm proves that task-performance gains can accompany real learning impairment, and population extrapolation (high school/math, K12, n=10 undergraduates) is highly risky; treating task performance as learning outcomes would systematically bias the evidence balance toward allowing use (skeptic task_vs_learning: high). (2) Disagreement with direct REJECT — E-003 has empirically shown that guardrails can combine practice gains with independent-exam safety (though only in the high-school mathematics context), and in 2026 students can access GPT-5-class tools without barriers; an outright ban lacks evidential necessity, is hard to enforce, and would abandon the opportunity to collect evidence in this context under controlled conditions. (3) Disagreement with insufficient_evidence (maintain the status quo, do nothing) — the evidence is not blank: E-002/E-003 provide high-quality policy-comparison anchors that directly inform a 'guardrails + no-AI independent assessment' pilot design; doing nothing is also a decision made on an evidence gap, but it forfeits the chance to re-validate E-003's guardrail effect in the C context, whereas the frame already provides a complete design with randomization, stop points, and independent assessment, keeping the pilot's execution cost and risk under control.

applicability.suitable_for: A limited-scale pilot with explicit guardrail design: random assignment (or quasi-experimental control within the same class), prohibition of directly submitting AI code, teacher-designed prompt guidance, on-demand weekly lab use with usage logging, the end-of-term no-AI unified machine-based and written exams as the sole learning-outcome criterion (non-inferiority success condition), and a mid-term no-AI independent quiz as a stop-loss point; pilot conclusions can guide introduction-rule design for the same university and course context
applicability.not_suitable_for: Unguardrailed, unfettered use (E-002 empirically demonstrates harm); using AI-present task performance such as homework completion rate or completion speed as effectiveness publicity or success criteria; elevating n=10/n=3 small-sample positive effects and qualitative themes to policy basis for 'AI introduction is net beneficial'; directly generalizing pilot results to other courses (e.g., data structures, algorithms) or the whole university; extrapolating effect sizes for the 2026 tool environment from 2023-2025 tool-generation evidence
required_conditions: Guardrails must be implemented: prohibit submitting AI-generated code directly as homework answers; guided usage rules (debugging errors, explaining concepts, code walkthroughs, refactoring suggestions); teacher involvement in prompt design — matching E-003's guardrail conditions

No-AI independent assessment system: no-AI machine-based pre-test at term start, mid-term no-AI independent quiz (stop-loss point), end-of-term no-AI unified machine-based and written exams, with grading and proctoring mechanisms excluding AI access

Randomized controlled or quasi-experimental design: random assignment of parallel classes in the same major / within the same class; identical content, workload, and instructor effort across groups, differing only in the AI policy; sample size determined by a power analysis referencing Bastani's -17% effect size

Non-inferiority success condition: only if the treatment group's end-of-term independent scores are not significantly lower than the control group is the introduction judged net beneficial; a significant negative effect triggers tightening or revocation of the allow policy
Process monitoring: log tool versions, usage scenarios, and frequency; report each group's actual AI usage and control-group compliance (contamination check)

Metacognitive support: comparison of self-assessment vs. actual scores and independent quizzes before/after AI assistance; identify strugglers and provide differentiated support (addressing E-008 illusion of competence and E-009 differentiation risk)
Reporting standards: explicit dropout rates, missing-data handling, and intention-to-treat analysis; transparent teacher assignment and prompt design; validate guardrail replicability across teachers

exceeds_evidence_boundary: Claiming guardrails necessarily eliminate the independent-exam negative effect in the C introductory context — E-003 was only validated in a single context (high-school mathematics, teacher-designed prompts); this adjudication only asserts that 'guardrail conditions are worth testing in the pilot'

Claiming learning improvement or retention within the 16-week semester — no semester-level evidence exists; all intervention windows are ≤4 sessions / single sessions / short training periods, and this adjudication does not presume the pilot outcome direction

Counting E-001/E-004/E-011/E-012's AI-present task performance as learning outcomes — this adjudication explicitly classifies them as task performance, supporting only 'AI present improves task performance'
Using E-006/E-007 (n=3 EFL writing qualitative) and E-011/E-012 (n=10 brownfield) as quantitative policy basis — they serve only as pedagogical design cues
Using E-010 (Denny review, UNSUPPORTED, abstract-only verification) as quantitative evidence that 'assessment is broken' — this item carries no evidential function
Extrapolating 2023-2025 tool-generation effect sizes to GPT-5-class agent environments — this adjudication only flags tool-generation drift risk and requires version logging in the pilot
Claiming a direction for cross-course transfer (e.g., subsequent data structures performance) — no transfer measurement evidence exists; the frame's secondary tracking is data yet to be collected

Claiming an overall judgment of 'AI introduction is net beneficial' or 'net harmful' — the evidence only supports 'effects depend on usage-rule design'; no directional judgment is made before pilot results

claims.claim: In practice sessions, the unguardrailed GPT Base (a standard ChatGPT-like interface) improved high-school students' practice scores by 48% relative to the control group, while the guardrailed GPT Tutor improved them by 127% (Table 1: practice coefficients 0.137/0.361, control mean 0.284)

On the unaided independent exam after AI access was removed, the GPT Base group scored 17% lower than the control group that never used AI (statistically significant), showing that unguardrailed AI use harms skill acquisition; mechanistically, students used GPT as a crutch and copied answers directly (GPT Base answered only 51% correctly, of which 42% were logic errors and 8% arithmetic errors), and students were overly optimistic in self-assessment, failing to notice the learning impairment

The guardrailed GPT Tutor (teacher-designed prompts instead of direct answers) improved practice scores by 127% while the negative effect on independent exams after access removal was essentially eliminated (-0.004, not significant), showing that carefully designed guardrails can combine practice gains with learning retention
Novices aged 10-17 who used OpenAI Codex during training performed significantly better on 45 Python code-writing tasks: completion rate improved 1.15x and scores 1.8x

Learners who used Codex during training scored slightly better than the control group on a one-week delayed post-test, but the difference was not statistically significant (no significant retention difference); among high Scratch pre-test scorers, those with Codex usage history did significantly better on the retention post-test

In a qualitative case study, 3 EFL students valued ChatGPT's assistance (reducing uncertainty, clarifying vocabulary, providing content suggestions, grammar/structure feedback that let them focus on the creative level) and developed strategies such as language refinement, idea generation and structuring, and proofreading and confidence building

In the same qualitative study, students worried about academic authenticity and over-reliance risks of AI use (limitations such as overly complex/formal suggestions, mismatched tone, cultural stereotypes), emphasized the need to keep human judgment and seek teacher/peer feedback, and called for ethical guidelines and critical-thinking cultivation

21 lab sessions (participant observation + interviews + eye tracking, 20/21 completing programming tasks) show that GenAI amplifies struggling novices' existing metacognitive difficulties and introduces new ones; students show cognitive dissonance and an 'illusion of competence' (believing they performed better than they actually did)

GenAI usage benefits are highly differentiated (widening gap): accelerators benefit by using GenAI to produce code they intended to write anyway and ignoring erroneous/irrelevant inline suggestions, while strugglers keep struggling; the gap between novices and more experienced/stronger students widens

Code generation models can already generate source code from natural-language problem descriptions with high accuracy, and their broad availability challenges homework and assessment in introductory programming classrooms, prompting computing educators to redesign teaching practice (framework review position, no primary data, background only)
10 undergraduate computer science students using GitHub Copilot on brownfield programming tasks (adding code to an unfamiliar legacy web codebase) completed tasks 35% faster (p<0.05)
With Copilot, students' solution progress was 50% greater (p<0.05), manual code-writing time was 11% lower (p<0.05), and web-search time was 12% lower (p<0.05)

In exit interviews, students expressed concerns about not understanding 'how/why' Copilot suggestions work; the study calls on computing educators to design pedagogies that harness GenAI benefits while promoting reflection on the principles behind suggestions

sources.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics

extensions.search_snippet: Anchor paper; abstract read and verified directly. Core evidence for comparing unguardrailed vs. guardrailed AI use on learning (note: population is high-school students; extrapolate to first-year university students with caution).
