control_group.note: All quantitative studies in the evidence set that make causal claims include a control condition: Bastani (E-001/E-002/E-003) is a three-arm RCT (unguardrailed GPT Base / guardrailed GPT Tutor / no-AI control, N=2848); Kazemitabaar (E-004/E-005) is a randomized comparison (with/without Codex, n=69); Shihab (E-011/E-012/E-013) is a within-subject comparison (same students with/without Copilot, n=10). The only studies without controls are qualitative/observational studies that make no causal claims (Marzuki E-006/E-007 n=3 cases, Prather E-008/E-009 21 observational sessions) and the review (Denny E-010), which pose no threat to the causal dimension. However, the population-closest empirical studies (Prather, Marzuki) are precisely the uncontrolled ones; treating their themes as effect evidence downstream would overstep.

randomization.note: Only the two largest studies used random assignment: Bastani (in-class random assignment, ~1000 students, E-001/E-002/E-003) and Kazemitabaar (randomized comparison, n=69, E-004/E-005). Shihab (E-011/E-012/E-013) uses a within-subject design without random assignment, compounded by task order and learning effects; Marzuki (E-006/E-007) and Prather (E-008/E-009) are non-experimental. The best-randomized studies are precisely the population-mismatched ones (high school/math), while the population-relevant studies have no randomization at all.

pre_test.note: Kazemitabaar explicitly reports a Scratch pre-test used for heterogeneity analysis (E-005: high pre-test scorers with Codex history did significantly better on the retention post-test); Bastani controls for baseline via a regression control mean (0.284) (E-001), but the evidence record does not detail an independent pre-test procedure or between-group baseline-equivalence testing; Shihab (E-011/E-012) substitutes 'highly similar tasks' for a pre-test with no true baseline measurement; Marzuki/Prather/Denny not applicable. Baseline control is overall unsystematic, and positive effects may partly reflect baseline differences.

post_test.note: Bastani set an independent exam after AI removal (E-002: GPT Base group -17% significant; E-003: Tutor group -0.004 not significant), the most rigorously designed post-test in the set; Kazemitabaar has a one-week delayed post-test (E-005). But Shihab (E-011/E-012) measured task performance only under AI-present conditions, with no no-AI independent post-test; Marzuki/Prather have no quantitative post-test. All positive-effect evidence (E-001/E-004/E-011/E-012) lacks this critical 'no-AI independent post-test' control.

retention_test.note: Only Kazemitabaar provides a true delayed retention measurement (one-week delayed post-test, null result, E-005); Bastani's independent exam immediately follows AI removal (immediate measurement, E-002/E-003), measuring near transfer rather than semester-level retention; Shihab, Marzuki, and Prather have no retention data. No study covers a time scale comparable to the 16-week pilot semester; evidence on long-term retention (even final exams, let alone subsequent courses) is entirely absent.

transfer_test.note: The most valuable transfer form — from 'AI-present practice' to 'no-AI independent performance' — is measured in Bastani (E-002/E-003) and Kazemitabaar (E-005), directly corresponding to the pilot's success criterion (end-of-term no-AI machine-based/written exam). But both studies have limited transfer distance (same domain, same problem type); there is no cross-task-type or cross-course (e.g., data structures) transfer measurement; Shihab (E-011/E-012) switches tool conditions in the same environment without measuring transfer; the frame's secondary tracking (subsequent course performance) has no evidence base supporting its expected direction.

sample_bias.note: Sample composition is systematically misaligned with the target population (domestic first-year zero-baseline C freshmen): Bastani (E-001~E-003) is Turkish 9-11 grade high-school mathematics; Kazemitabaar (E-004/E-005) is 10-17-year-old K12 programming novices; Marzuki (E-006/E-007) is EFL academic writing; the only undergraduate sample, Shihab (E-011~E-013), is n=10 with brownfield web codebase tasks (not zero-baseline C introductory); Prather (E-008/E-009) targets introductory-course novices but is observational. Extrapolation must cross two dimensions — 'high school to university' and 'math/web to C introductory' — and no single study matches both domain and age level.

self_selection.note: Bastani used in-class random assignment (E-001~E-003), minimizing self-selection bias; it is the cleanest sample in the set. Kazemitabaar (E-004/E-005) recruited participants in an after-school program, introducing some self-selection; Shihab (E-011~E-013) had all n=10 volunteers, and volunteers tend to be more proactive with higher technology acceptance, so the positive speed/progress effects may be overestimated; Marzuki (E-006/E-007) used purposive sampling/volunteer interviews, and the 'valuing AI assistance' theme cannot be extrapolated. Self-selection bias is inversely related to population relevance: the more relevant the sample, the stronger the self-selection.

measurement_validity.note: The validity of completion rate/correctness/speed as proxies for 'learning' is questionable: E-001 practice correctness, E-004 task scores, and E-011/E-012 completion speed and progress are all measured under AI-accessible conditions, where AI can directly produce answers and inflate the metrics, making it impossible to distinguish 'learned' from 'copied' (Bastani mechanism data E-002: 42% of GPT Base's 51% correct answers were logic errors; Wermelinger S-2023 shows Copilot solved 16 of 24 typical introductory problems on first attempt, FETCH_PARTIAL verified only to the institutional repository abstract). Self-report measures are unreliable (E-002 students overly optimistic, E-008 illusion of competence). The higher-validity measurements (no-AI independent exams E-002/E-003, delayed post-test E-005) are precisely the ones giving negative or null results — measurement choice itself determines the conclusion direction.

confounders.note: Bastani (E-001~E-003) is best controlled (same classroom environment, fixed session duration) but still has motivation/engagement differences and confounding from the extra instructional input of teacher-designed prompts in the guardrail group. Shihab (E-011/E-012) within-subject design stacks order effects, learning effects, and fatigue ('highly similar tasks' are necessarily faster the second time); Kazemitabaar (E-004/E-005) after-school program has practice-amount/supervision differences. No study systematically controls practice time, motivation, or peer effects.

instructor_effect.note: The evidence record reports no teacher/TA difference control in any study: Bastani's guardrail condition depends on 'teacher-designed prompts' (E-003), confounding prompt quality with guardrail effectiveness, so 'guardrails work' cannot be separated from 'good teachers work'; Kazemitabaar's after-school program may have a single mentor; Shihab is a single-researcher environment (constant instructor but single sample). For the pilot, guardrail replicability depends on teachers' ability to design prompts, and this condition-dependence was not separated and tested in any study.

novelty_effect.note: All positive effects come from short interventions and novelty effects cannot be excluded: Bastani had only 4 in-class 90-minute sessions (E-001 +48%/+127%, E-002 independent exam immediately after); Kazemitabaar training-period tasks (E-004) and one-week post-test (E-005); Shihab single lab session (E-011/E-012). No study covers a 16-week semester cycle; there is no evidence on long-term engagement or maintenance of learning effects after novelty fades; the skeptic's novelty_effect check is also a medium risk.

tool_version_effect.note: The evidence tool generation differs from the pilot tool generation: Kazemitabaar (E-004/E-005) used 2023 OpenAI Codex (code-davinci era), Marzuki (E-006/E-007) GPT-3.5/4-era ChatGPT, Bastani (E-001~E-003) GPT-4 era, Shihab (E-011~E-013) 2024-2025 Copilot; in the pilot year (2025-2026) students face GPT-5-class models and deeply IDE-integrated agents — more capable and more deeply integrated, potentially amplifying both benefits and dependency risks, so 2023-2025 effect sizes cannot be directly extrapolated.

ai_usage_policy.note: Bastani (E-001~E-003) is the only study directly manipulating AI usage policy: unguardrailed GPT Base (standard ChatGPT-like interface, answers copyable) vs. guardrailed GPT Tutor (teacher-designed prompts, no direct answers), empirically demonstrating the policy contrast 'allowed but unruled → -17% independent-exam harm' and 'guardrailed → +127% practice with the negative effect eliminated', structurally isomorphic to the pilot's guardrail design ('no direct submission of AI code, independent assessment in lab'). Limitations: the guardrail effect was validated in a single context (high-school math, teacher-designed prompts) and needs replication in the C context; and no study verified control-group compliance (whether control members actually refrained from AI), so policy contamination is not excluded.

dropout.note: The evidence record does not report dropout rates, missing-data handling, or compliance verification for each study: Bastani's ~1000 students, 4 sessions, 2,848 observations (E-001~E-003) do not state attrition across sessions or missingness; Kazemitabaar n=69 one-week post-test (E-005) retention rate not reported; Shihab n=10 completed all tasks and attended exit interviews (E-011~E-013), the only study where low dropout can be inferred; Marzuki n=3 interview sample. Intention-to-treat vs. actual-use (control secretly using AI) compliance analysis is absent across the set.

task_vs_learning_guard.measured_construct: The evidence set measures two distinct constructs: (1) AI-present task performance — E-001 practice scores (+48%/+127%), E-004 training-period completion rate/scores (+1.15x/+1.8x), E-011/E-012 completion speed (35% faster) and progress (50% more), all measured under AI-accessible conditions where AI can directly produce results; (2) post-AI-removal independent learning outcomes — E-002 independent exam -17% (significant), E-003 independent exam -0.004 (not significant), E-005 one-week delayed post-test (null).
task_vs_learning_guard.note: The evidence set itself does not equate task performance with learning outcomes: the three independent measurements (E-002/E-003/E-005) are explicitly separated from the task-performance measurements (E-001/E-004/E-011/E-012), and the independent measurements give negative/null results — a correct execution of the control rule (SKILL.md RULE 3: task performance must not be automatically equated with learning effect). But the risk sits at the boundary: (a) if downstream synthesis uses E-001's +127% or E-011's 35% faster as 'learning gain' evidence, the rule is violated and the evidence balance systematically tilts toward 'allow use'; (b) E-001's practice gains and E-002's independent-exam harm coexist in the same study, and citing only one is misleading. The frame's outcomes already measure 'task performance' and 'learning ability' separately and set the end-of-term no-AI unified machine-based/written exam as the sole success criterion, consistent with this guard.

limitations: Population and domain mismatch: no study directly covers 'first-year zero-baseline C freshmen + full semester'; extrapolation must cross high school → university and math/web → C introductory, with high external-validity risk (skeptic population_external_validity: high)

The population-relevant studies have extremely small samples and weak designs: Shihab n=10 within-subject (fragile p<0.05 compounded by order/learning effects), Marzuki n=3 qualitative cases, Prather 21 observational sessions without controls — the strongest evidence comes from the population-mismatched study (Bastani high-school/math RCT), and the best-matched population has the least reliable evidence
Positive effects are mostly AI-present task-performance proxies rather than no-AI independent learning measurements; the higher-validity measurements (E-002/E-003/E-005) give negative or null results

All intervention windows are short (≤4 90-minute sessions / single session / short training period); no 16-week semester-level data; novelty effects cannot be excluded; long-term retention and transfer evidence is absent

Tool-generation drift: 2023-2025 evidence is based on Codex/GPT-3.5-4 generation tools, while the pilot year uses GPT-5-class agents deeply integrated with IDEs; effect sizes cannot be directly extrapolated
Retention measurement is weak: only Kazemitabaar has a 1-week delayed post-test (null); Bastani's independent exam is an immediate measurement; no cross-course (data structures) tracking evidence
The evidence record does not report dropout rates, missing-data handling, or control-group compliance (whether controls actually refrained from AI); policy contamination risk is untested

Bastani's guardrail effect depends on teacher-designed prompts; teacher quality and guardrail design are confounded, and guardrail replicability was not separately validated; the effect was validated only in high-school mathematics

Wermelinger (Copilot 16/24 introductory problems) is only FETCH_PARTIAL (institutional repository abstract page, oro.open.ac.uk fallback); full-text verification is insufficient, and the assessment-distortion argument relies on abstract content

Shihab's 35%/50% speed and progress gains are from brownfield tasks (legacy web codebase), which do not match first-year C introductory task types; they can serve only as pedagogical design cues, not as quantitative basis for 'AI introduction is net beneficial'
suggestions: Maintain and strengthen the frame's randomized controlled design: random assignment within class/grade + no-AI machine-based pre-test at term start + end-of-term no-AI unified machine-based and written exams with the same paper, with non-inferiority as the success condition (treatment not significantly worse than control); sample size via power analysis referencing Bastani's -17% effect size, avoiding n=10-class samples

Adopt a three-arm design replicating Bastani's policy contrast: unguardrailed group (standard AI interface) / guardrailed group (teacher-designed prompts, no direct submission of AI code) / control group, directly validating in the C context whether guardrails combine practice gains with independent-exam safety

Make independent measurement the sole learning-outcome criterion: AI-present task performance such as homework/lab completion rate and completion speed are process indicators reported separately and explicitly labeled 'task performance'; writing them into 'learning gain' conclusions is prohibited; citing such metrics in publicity or mid-term reports systematically overestimates benefits

Add a mid-term stop-loss point: schedule a no-AI mid-term independent quiz around week 8; if the treatment group shows a significant negative effect (Bastani -17% magnitude), immediately tighten or suspend the allow policy

Add retention and transfer measurement: delayed retest 2-4 weeks after term end, and include subsequent course (data structures) performance in tracking (the frame's secondary design needs data collection implemented)

Log tool versions and usage scenarios (the frame's frequency/log design should be enforced); assess mid-term whether guardrails need adjustment for tool generation; report each group's actual AI usage and control-group compliance (contamination check)

Pair metacognitive interventions and detection: following Prather's (E-008/E-009) illusion-of-competence and differentiation evidence, add self-assessment vs. actual score comparisons and independent quizzes before/after AI assistance to identify strugglers and provide differentiated support

Reporting standards: explicit dropout rates, missing-data handling, intention-to-treat analysis; transparent teacher assignment and prompt-design process (addressing instructor_effect confounding); ideally validate guardrail replicability across ≥2 teachers/classes

conflicts.reason_for_disagreement: This adjudication clearly disagrees with three alternative positions: (1) Disagreement with direct ADOPT — the E-001 +127% and E-011 35% faster figures cited by those who claim 'allowing use is net beneficial' are all AI-present task performance; within the same study, E-002's -17% independent-exam harm proves that task-performance gains can accompany real learning impairment, and population extrapolation (high school/math, K12, n=10 undergraduates) is highly risky; treating task performance as learning outcomes would systematically bias the evidence balance toward allowing use (skeptic task_vs_learning: high). (2) Disagreement with direct REJECT — E-003 has empirically shown that guardrails can combine practice gains with independent-exam safety (though only in the high-school mathematics context), and in 2026 students can access GPT-5-class tools without barriers; an outright ban lacks evidential necessity, is hard to enforce, and would abandon the opportunity to collect evidence in this context under controlled conditions. (3) Disagreement with insufficient_evidence (maintain the status quo, do nothing) — the evidence is not blank: E-002/E-003 provide high-quality policy-comparison anchors that directly inform a 'guardrails + no-AI independent assessment' pilot design; doing nothing is also a decision made on an evidence gap, but it forfeits the chance to re-validate E-003's guardrail effect in the C context, whereas the frame already provides a complete design with randomization, stop points, and independent assessment, keeping the pilot's execution cost and risk under control.

applicability.suitable_for: A limited-scale pilot with explicit guardrail design: random assignment (or quasi-experimental control within the same class), prohibition of directly submitting AI code, teacher-designed prompt guidance, on-demand weekly lab use with usage logging, the end-of-term no-AI unified machine-based and written exams as the sole learning-outcome criterion (non-inferiority success condition), and a mid-term no-AI independent quiz as a stop-loss point; pilot conclusions can guide introduction-rule design for the same university and course context
applicability.not_suitable_for: Unguardrailed, unfettered use (E-002 empirically demonstrates harm); using AI-present task performance such as homework completion rate or completion speed as effectiveness publicity or success criteria; elevating n=10/n=3 small-sample positive effects and qualitative themes to policy basis for 'AI introduction is net beneficial'; directly generalizing pilot results to other courses (e.g., data structures, algorithms) or the whole university; extrapolating effect sizes for the 2026 tool environment from 2023-2025 tool-generation evidence
required_conditions: Guardrails must be implemented: prohibit submitting AI-generated code directly as homework answers; guided usage rules (debugging errors, explaining concepts, code walkthroughs, refactoring suggestions); teacher involvement in prompt design — matching E-003's guardrail conditions

No-AI independent assessment system: no-AI machine-based pre-test at term start, mid-term no-AI independent quiz (stop-loss point), end-of-term no-AI unified machine-based and written exams, with grading and proctoring mechanisms excluding AI access

Randomized controlled or quasi-experimental design: random assignment of parallel classes in the same major / within the same class; identical content, workload, and instructor effort across groups, differing only in the AI policy; sample size determined by a power analysis referencing Bastani's -17% effect size

Non-inferiority success condition: only if the treatment group's end-of-term independent scores are not significantly lower than the control group is the introduction judged net beneficial; a significant negative effect triggers tightening or revocation of the allow policy
Process monitoring: log tool versions, usage scenarios, and frequency; report each group's actual AI usage and control-group compliance (contamination check)

Metacognitive support: comparison of self-assessment vs. actual scores and independent quizzes before/after AI assistance; identify strugglers and provide differentiated support (addressing E-008 illusion of competence and E-009 differentiation risk)
Reporting standards: explicit dropout rates, missing-data handling, and intention-to-treat analysis; transparent teacher assignment and prompt design; validate guardrail replicability across teachers

intervention.target_learners: Zero-baseline freshmen majoring in Computer Science and Technology at our university (taking C Programming for the first time this semester, no systematic programming experience before enrollment, no programming-competition participation), with wide variation in motivation and self-discipline, high curiosity about AI tools, and limited English proficiency for some students. The pilot uses in-class random assignment: parallel classes in the same major are randomly divided into a treatment group (guardrailed, phased-in AI use) and a control group (traditional teaching, AI fully banned), with identical content, workload, and instructor effort across groups.
learning_goals: Master C core syntax and programming fundamentals: variables and data types, control flow, functions, arrays, pointers, structs; independently write programs up to 200 lines
Build independent debugging ability: autonomously read compile errors and runtime errors, locate and fix logic errors, and complete the debugging loop without relying on AI
Develop independent programming and problem-solving ability in no-AI environments (end-of-term unified machine-based exam is a hard assessment)
Learn to use AI tools critically: judge whether AI output is correct, explain the rationale for adopted suggestions, understand and comply with the 'prompts not answers' guardrail rules
Develop metacognitive monitoring: accurately estimate one's own ability level, identify and correct 'illusion of competence' (deviation between self-assessment and independent quiz results)
Use generative AI responsibly: log usage scenarios, reflect on learning gains, and never submit AI-generated code directly as homework
intervention.pilot_duration: First semester of academic year 2025-2026, 16-week teaching cycle (2 credit hours of theory + 2 hours of lab per week), co-extensive with the course; after the end-of-term unified machine-based and written exams, one delayed retention test is added (week 4 after the intervention ends) to measure retention.

phase_1.name: No-generation phase: hand-written fundamentals (weeks 1-4)
activities: All code written by hand: syntax introduction, variables and expressions, control flow; the full compile-and-run loop completed manually with no AI assistance of any kind

Error-reading training: the teacher demonstrates how to read compile error line numbers and hints; students keep a personal 'error log' (original error text + own troubleshooting process + final cause)
At the end of week 4, the course's first no-AI independent quiz (variables, branches, loops, 8-10 problems) serves as the semester baseline
The teacher explains the course AI policy and the guardrail rules for each subsequent phase; students sign informed consent and usage-log commitments
phase_1.ai_usage_rule: Generative AI coding assistants are completely banned (Copilot, ChatGPT/Claude code generation, Cursor autocomplete, and all other forms). For errors and conceptual questions, students must first troubleshoot independently or consult the teacher/classmates; the goal is to build syntax sensitivity and the most basic debugging loop under no-AI conditions, forming the foundation for judging AI output correctness in later phases.
phase_1.outcome_check: Week-4 no-AI independent quiz score is baseline B0; the treatment and control groups should show no significant difference (validating random assignment); error-log submission rate and quality enter the process record.

phase_2.name: Explanation phase: prompts not answers (weeks 5-8)
activities: Introduce AI use strictly limited to the 'explainer' role: explain concepts (what a pointer is, how the function call stack works), explain error meanings, and explain given code snippets line by line

The teacher designs and provides Socratic prompt templates ('My code reports error Y on line X, I have already checked Z — what could be the cause?' 'Please explain the execution of this while loop, do not give me new code'); students must ask within the template structure

Pre-question requirement: students must first write out their own attempt, sticking point, and hypothesis before asking AI; if AI output contains code snippets, students must close AI, retype the code themselves, and explain it line by line
Lab sessions include a fixed weekly 30-minute no-AI independent programming segment alternating with AI-use segments
At the end of week 8: mid-term no-AI independent quiz (functions, arrays, pointers, comprehensive problems); the teacher reviews prompt quality in usage logs
phase_2.ai_usage_rule: Only 'explain/locate/hint'-type outputs may be requested; requesting code generation or direct answers in any form is prohibited (this is the guardrail core validated by Bastani E-003: no direct answers, only guiding hints). Copying and pasting AI output into the editor is prohibited; all code produced with AI assistance must be rewritten by the student. Weekly usage logs record: tool and version, question scenario, prompt text, AI answer key points, personal gains and confusion.
phase_2.outcome_check: Mid-term independent quiz score M1 vs. baseline B0; non-inferiority test between treatment and control; log-review pass rate (share of rule-violating code-request prompts <10%) as guardrail enforcement indicator; self-assessment vs. measured deviation recording begins (see illusion-of-competence monitoring).

phase_3.name: Collaboration phase: walkthroughs and refactoring (weeks 9-13)
activities: Use AI to walk through one's own code (locate bug positions, point out edge-case omissions, suggest refactorings), but every adopted suggestion must include a 'rationale for adoption' (why it is correct, why adopted, why not adopted)
Staged small-project homework (comprehensive use of arrays/pointers/structs, ~150-200 lines): design → hand-written implementation → AI walkthrough → revision → reflection, a five-step submission
Pair review: students walk through each other's code and compare 'human review' vs. 'AI review' differences to train critical evaluation of AI output
Weekly 30-minute no-AI independent programming segments continue, with difficulty increasing as the course progresses

For strugglers in the bottom 20% of weekly no-AI quiz rankings: individual teacher tutoring with AI permissions downgraded (back to explanation-phase rules; walkthrough/refactoring use banned); for top-20% accelerators: stay within collaboration-phase rules, no early unlocking of any 'generate code' permission
At the end of week 13: third no-AI independent quiz (full-range comprehensive problems)
phase_3.ai_usage_rule: AI may review, locate, explain, and suggest refactorings, but the body of homework code must be written by the student; submitting an entire AI-generated code block directly counts as a violation (one warning, zero score on second offense, disqualification from the treatment group on third). Any adopted AI suggestion must include an explanation. Weekly usage logs and reflections continue; tool versions (including model generation) must be registered.
phase_3.outcome_check: Third independent quiz M2 between-group comparison (continued non-inferiority monitoring); whether the struggler intervention group (bottom 20%) recovers on independent quizzes as a differentiation-control indicator; homework similarity checks (preventing direct AI submission) with zero violations.

phase_4.name: Transfer phase: no-AI independent assessment (weeks 14-16 + week-20 delayed test)
activities: Full AI withdrawal: from week 14, both treatment and control groups enter no-AI review and mock machine-based exam sessions, practicing comprehensive programming in no-AI environments (simulating final-exam problem types and duration)

End-of-term unified machine-based exam (no-AI computer room: offline, all AI tools and external peripherals banned, randomized problem order, code-similarity detection) and unified written exam (concepts, program reading, error fixing)
Week 4 after the final exam (week 20): delayed retention test (independently completing 2 comprehensive programming problems) to measure retention
Whole-group end-of-term self-assessment questionnaire (self-estimated final machine-based score range) compared against measured scores to produce the illusion-of-competence indicator
phase_4.ai_usage_rule: AI is completely banned (same condition as the control group). This phase measures 'the ability to complete tasks independently after AI removal', the only valid learning-outcome criterion.
phase_4.outcome_check: Final machine-based + written exams: non-inferiority test of treatment vs. control (primary criterion; preregistered threshold: effect-size d confidence-interval lower bound not below -0.2 for non-inferiority, significant superiority for superiority); delayed retention test between-group comparison (secondary); self-assessment vs. measured deviation magnitude (illusion-of-competence indicator) between-group comparison.

intervention.ai_usage_policy: Phased progressive-access scheme: AI permissions open gradually across 4 phases (no-generation → explanation → collaboration → no-AI transfer assessment); failing an independent quiz/guardrail enforcement check in any phase prevents early unlocking of the next. Guardrail core is 'prompts not answers': teacher-designed prompt templates; AI may only explain, locate, and guide — generating code or direct answers is prohibited; AI-output code must be explained and then rewritten by the student. Homework may not directly submit AI-generated code; weekly 30-minute no-AI independent programming runs through weeks 1-13; mandatory weekly usage logs (tool and version, scenario, prompt, reflection) reviewed by the teacher; the end-of-term no-AI unified machine-based and written exams are the sole learning-outcome criterion, and routine homework/lab completion rates and AI-present task performance are never treated as learning-outcome evidence.
intervention.teacher_role: Design each phase's guardrail rules and Socratic prompt templates (matching the 'teacher-designed prompts' validation condition in Bastani E-003); review student usage logs and prompt quality weekly, identifying and interviewing violators and self-assessment-overestimating students; organize weekly no-AI independent quizzes and analyze between-group differences; implement downgrade interventions and individual tutoring for bottom-20% strugglers and prevent top-20% accelerators from outsourcing to AI; assess tool-generation changes mid-term and decide whether to adjust guardrails; in mid-term reports cite only no-AI independent measurements and refuse to cite task-performance metrics.
intervention.student_role: Comply with phase-access rules and the 'prompts not answers' guardrail; write out one's own attempt, sticking point, and hypothesis before asking; rewrite AI-output code by hand and explain it line by line; fill in a rationale for adopted AI suggestions; submit weekly usage logs and reflections; participate in weekly no-AI independent programming and each phase's independent quizzes; honestly estimate one's level in end-of-term self-assessment and accept self-assessment-vs-measured feedback.
intervention.reflection_requirement: Weekly reflection log: this week's AI usage scenarios, question-and-answer key points, new knowledge learned, unresolved problems, and independent-quiz impressions. At the end of each phase, submit an 'ability self-assessment' (estimated score for independently completing that phase's problems without AI); the teacher compares it against the independent-quiz measured score and feeds back to the student — self-assessment overestimation by more than one level triggers an individual talk (countering illusion of competence). 'Rationale for adoption' is mandatory when adopting AI suggestions (forcing reflection on 'why it is correct', addressing the risk that students do not understand AI suggestion principles).
intervention.assessment: Primary criterion (sole learning-outcome basis): end-of-term unified machine-based + written exams, non-inferiority test of treatment vs. control (preregistered: d confidence-interval lower bound ≥ -0.2 for non-inferiority, significantly positive for superiority); the machine-based exam runs in a no-AI computer room with randomized problem order and code-similarity detection excluding AI access and ghost-writing. Secondary indicators: no-AI independent quiz trajectories across phases (B0 → M1 → M2 → final, between- and within-group); delayed retention test in week 4 after the final (retention); AI usage logs and prompt-quality scores (guardrail enforcement); self-assessment vs. measured deviation (illusion-of-competence indicator); struggler/accelerator group trajectories (differentiation monitoring). Explicitly non-evidence indicators: homework completion rate, lab completion speed, and AI-present task performance (per the 'task performance ≠ learning' review conclusion).
risk_control: Dependency risk (matching E-002 unguardrailed -17%): enforce the 'prompts not answers' guardrail (the only design validated to remove the negative effect, E-003), weekly 30-minute no-AI independent programming, phased progressive access rather than one-step opening, log monitoring of 'request code' prompt share (exceeding 10% triggers guardrail strengthening), and homework similarity detection preventing direct AI submission

Illusion-of-competence risk (matching E-008 and E-002's overly optimistic self-assessment): per-phase self-assessment vs. independent-quiz measured comparison feedback; overestimation beyond 1 level triggers an individual talk; mid-term reports exclude task-performance metrics to prevent systematic overestimation for both students and teachers

Differentiation risk (matching E-009 accelerator/struggler gap widening): weekly no-AI independent quiz rankings; bottom-20% strugglers get AI permission downgrades (back to explanation phase) + individual teacher tutoring; top-20% accelerators stay within collaboration-phase rules; observe whether the intervention narrows rather than widens within-group gaps

Assessment-integrity risk (matching measurement_validity and Wermelinger's assessment threat): the end-of-term no-AI machine-based/written exam is the sole learning-outcome criterion; the machine-based exam is offline with AI banned, randomized problem order + similarity detection; refusing to substitute homework completion rates for ability indicators

Self-selection risk (matching self_selection): in-class random assignment (same as Bastani's RCT design); the control group receives equal instructor effort and after-class Q&A resources; informed consent with full-group enrollment reduces volunteer bias

Tool-generation drift risk (matching tool_drift): mandatory registration of AI tool and model versions; mid-term assessment of how tool capability changes affect guardrails (stronger models may amplify both benefits and dependency risks); adjust prompt templates and phase boundaries if needed

Novelty-effect risk (matching novelty_effect): all positive effects are 'AI-present task performance' from short interventions; the pilot explicitly anchors on the full 16 weeks with no-AI independent measurement, and the 4-week no-generation phase doubles as a novelty cooling-off period

Evidence-extrapolation risk (matching population_external_validity and sample_size): small-sample positive effects (E-011 n=10, E-006 n=3) serve only as pedagogical design cues and are not written into introduction-policy grounds; the pilot itself fills the 'first-year zero-baseline C freshmen + full semester' evidence gap, hence strict non-inferiority success conditions and stop-loss points
stop_conditions: Mid-term (week 8) no-AI independent quiz: treatment group significantly below control (p<0.05 and effect size d<-0.2) → immediately tighten: downgrade treatment AI permissions to explanation-phase rules, retest two weeks later; if still significantly negative, the whole group returns to the no-generation phase
Any week's no-AI independent quiz shows a significant negative effect (between-group d<-0.2) → that week triggers a guardrail review; AI use is suspended that week until the cause is confirmed

Log review finds 'direct code request' prompt share above 10% for two consecutive weeks, or similarity detection confirms 3+ AI ghost-writing events → strengthen guardrails (tighten prompt templates, increase no-AI segment duration) and notify everyone

End-of-term unified machine-based/written exam non-inferiority test fails (d confidence-interval lower bound < -0.2) → pilot judged failed; next semester the allow policy is tightened or revoked with a full failure report
End-of-term delayed retention test shows treatment group significantly below control → even if the machine-based exam is non-inferior, retention risk is established and the policy stays tightened

Mid-term or end-of-term within-group differentiation significantly widens (bottom-20% gap vs. control bottom-20% widens with no intervention effect) → differentiation control fails; narrow AI use to the explanation phase only
Systematic cheating or proctoring breach at any point (AI access found in the machine-based exam) → immediately invalidate that session's scores and re-evaluate the assessment mechanism
evidence_alignment: Overall decision is pilot (minimum verifiable) rather than full introduction → E-001, E-002, E-003 (the only high-quality RCT shows the benefit of allowing use depends entirely on rule design, to be validated in our context); E-011, E-006 (small-sample evidence cannot be policy basis)
In-class random assignment + control class → E-001 (Bastani's in-class random assignment is the cleanest sample in the set, minimal self-selection)

Phase 1 no-generation period (hand-written fundamentals before AI contact) → E-002 (unguardrailed use caused -17% on independent exams; students used AI as a crutch); E-008 (novices' metacognitive difficulties amplified by AI; basics and monitoring habits must be built first)

Phase 2 explanation-period 'prompts not answers' guardrail (teacher-designed prompt templates, no direct answers) → E-003 (Bastani's guardrailed GPT Tutor improved practice by +127% while the independent-exam negative effect was eliminated to -0.004, not significant — the only design validated to remove the negative effect; needs replication in the C context)

Phase 3 collaboration-period walkthrough/refactoring with mandatory adoption rationale → E-013 (students report not understanding Copilot suggestion principles; forced explanation needed); E-011, E-012 (collaboration-scenario speed/progress gains are pedagogical cues only, not learning-outcome evidence)

Phase 4 no-AI transfer assessment + post-final delayed retention test → E-002, E-003 (post-AI-removal independent measurement is the validity-correct learning-outcome criterion); E-005 (Kazemitabaar measured null retention with a one-week delayed post-test; same-type measurement needed to verify retention)

Weekly 30-minute no-AI independent programming throughout → E-002 (crutch mechanism: AI-present correctness is inflated while ability is not acquired; periodic AI-free checks needed); E-003 (prerequisite for the guardrail group's retained ability)

Self-assessment vs. measured comparison and individual talks → E-008 (illusion of competence: believing performance exceeds actual); E-002 (GPT Base group overly optimistic self-assessment, failure to notice learning impairment)
Struggler downgrade interventions + accelerator limits → E-009 (GenAI benefits highly differentiated; strugglers keep struggling and gaps widen; targeted intervention needed)

End-of-term no-AI machine-based exam as sole criterion, rejecting task-performance metrics → corresponds to task_vs_learning and measurement_validity audits (E-001/E-004/E-011/E-012 are all AI-present task performance and cannot prove learning gains; E-002/E-003/E-005 are the learning-outcome measurements); Wermelinger assessment threat (homework completion rates invalidated)

Mandatory usage logs registering tool and model versions → E-011, E-012, E-013 (tool-generation drift: evidence is based on 2023-2025 tools; stronger 2026 models require mid-term guardrail re-evaluation)

Mid-term stop-loss points and strict non-inferiority success conditions → E-002 (-17% independent-exam harm is an empirical risk that must have a triggerable tightening threshold); E-003, E-005 (success criteria must be no-AI independent measurements); fills the population_external_validity evidence gap (no study directly covers first-year zero-baseline C freshmen + full semester)

evaluation.research_question: In the first-year C programming course, does allowing students to use generative AI coding assistants under guided rules (guardrails), relative to fully prohibiting use, improve the learning experience without harming (non-inferior to) students' no-AI independent programming ability, while controlling risks such as AI dependency and illusion of competence? Can the effects be maintained in semester-level retention and transfer (subsequent courses)?

groups.treatment: Treatment group (guardrailed): allowed to use generative AI coding assistants (Copilot/ChatGPT/Claude/Cursor, etc., per tools available to students), with usage limited to debugging errors, concept explanation, code walkthroughs, and refactoring suggestions; submitting AI-generated code directly as homework answers is prohibited; teacher-designed usage-guide prompts are provided (no direct answers, guided thinking); lab sessions include independent no-AI assessment segments. Continues for the full 16-week semester; all usage recorded via logs/self-report (frequency, scenario, tool version).
groups.comparison: Control group: traditional teaching with all generative AI coding assistants banned throughout; teaching content, workload, and instructor effort identical to the treatment group; compliance monitored via self-report and in-class spot checks (contamination check). The two groups are compared only on the end-of-term no-AI unified machine-based and written exams with the same paper, with a term-start same-paper pre-test controlling baseline.

evaluation.baseline: Weeks 1-2 no-AI machine-based pre-test: in an offline computer room with no AI tools (IDE plugins banned), students independently answer problems isomorphic to the final machine-based exam but of lower difficulty (expression evaluation, branch/loop basics, simple I/O, read-program-write-output), plus a small set of written conceptual questions. Purposes: (1) between-group baseline equivalence testing (t-test / standardized mean difference SMD < 0.2); (2) covariate for learning gain (post-test − baseline); (3) stratified heterogeneity analysis (low/mid/high baseline groups, following Kazemitabaar E-005 pre-test stratification). Scores count at zero or minimal weight toward the usual grade to avoid motivation contamination.
evaluation.post_test: Weeks 15-16 end-of-term no-AI unified machine-based + written exams (same paper, same proctoring environment for both groups): (1) machine-based: offline environment, independently complete comprehensive programming problems (arrays/strings, functions, pointers, structs); automatic test-case evaluation (objective correctness) + double-blind human grading of code quality (readability, structure, naming, no redundancy); (2) written: conceptual questions, read-program-write-output, program error fixing, simple algorithm design. The machine-based and written exams are the sole learning-outcome criteria, with AI banned throughout.
evaluation.retention_test: 2-4 weeks after term end (early winter break or weeks 1-2 of the next semester) no-AI delayed retest: a parallel paper of equivalent difficulty to the final machine-based exam (same problem types, new problems), plus written key-point retest, measuring semester-level retention rather than immediate near transfer — responding to the gap that only Kazemitabaar has 1-week retention data (E-005, null result) and Bastani has only immediate measurement (E-002/E-003).
evaluation.transfer_test: Two-channel transfer measurement: (1) task-type transfer — the retention test and final written exam include new task types not practiced (e.g., moving from writing to debugging and fixing given code, from algorithm problems to code completion and reading/explanation, from C concepts to pseudocode/C-like-language problems), testing cross-task generalization (responding to the limitation that Bastani/Kazemitabaar transfer distance is limited to the same domain and problem type); (2) cross-course transfer — no-AI assessment performance in the first 4-6 weeks of the next semester's data structures course (first periodic quiz and major assignment) as long-term transfer tracking (implementing the frame's secondary design).
process_metrics: Lab task completion rate and correctness (measured under AI-present conditions; task performance, not included in learning conclusions)
Task completion speed/duration (benchmarked against Bastani E-001 +48%/+127% and Shihab E-011/E-012 35% faster magnitudes; pedagogical cue only)
AI usage frequency: weekly usage count and session duration (tool logs + self-report cross-validated)
AI usage scenario distribution: share of debugging errors / concept explanation / code generation / refactoring suggestions
AI output acceptance and modification rates (whether adopted suggestions were modified with understanding)
Independent attempt duration and attempt count before asking AI (measuring think-first-then-ask)
Homework on-time submission rate and pass rate
Control-group AI usage (self-report + end-of-term anonymous questionnaire): contamination check for compliance analysis
Tool version and model registration (addressing tool-generation drift, responding to methodology tool_version_effect)
learning_metrics: End-of-term no-AI machine-based objective score (test-case pass rate/correctness) — primary criterion, following the Bastani E-002/E-003 independent-exam paradigm
End-of-term no-AI machine-based code quality human score (double-blind grading averaged)
End-of-term no-AI written exam score (conceptual understanding and error-fixing ability)
Mid-term (week 8) no-AI independent quiz score — mid-term stop-loss basis
Learning gain: post-test total − baseline pre-test total (gain score), compared between groups
Retention test score (delayed retest 2-4 weeks after term end)
Transfer test scores (new task types + data structures course performance)

All of the above are collected in no-AI independent assessment environments; any metric measured under AI-present conditions is classified into process_metrics and never enters learning-outcome conclusions (task_vs_learning separation rule)
risk_metrics: No-AI independent task completion rate: share of tasks fully completed independently (without asking) in mid-term/final independent assessments, compared against baseline (the frame success_condition's core risk indicator)

Illusion of competence (Prather E-008): self-assessed score vs. actual score difference (overconfidence gap) before each independent assessment, tracked across the semester; self-assessment after AI-assisted tasks vs. subsequent no-AI independent quiz scores
AI-dependency self-rating scale: anxiety/confidence when away from AI, tendency to ask AI before attempting tasks (5-point Likert, once at mid-term and once at final)
Over-reliance behavior: share of homework containing directly submitted AI-generated code without understanding (guardrail violation rate), share of AI outputs adopted without reading
Differentiation risk (Prather E-009 widening gap): relative performance of baseline-low groups on no-AI post-tests vs. high groups, testing whether the gap widens

Metacognitive indicator: ability to explain in one's own words how AI suggestions work (mid-term sampling + final oral exam, responding to Shihab E-013 students' not understanding 'how/why' suggestions work)

Over-optimism monitoring: combining E-002's mechanism of students not noticing learning impairment, the correlation between self-assessment-actual difference and independent scores enters the risk report
evaluation.analysis_plan: Design: within-class/parallel-class random assignment (or quasi-experiment with baseline equivalence); sample size via power analysis referencing Bastani's independent-exam -17% effect size (α=0.05, power=0.80, non-inferiority margin 0.3 standard deviations), avoiding n=10-class samples. Primary analysis: between-group non-inferiority test of end-of-term no-AI machine-based + written total scores (one-sided, H0: treatment worse than control ≥ margin), supplemented by ANCOVA (baseline pre-test as covariate) and mixed-effects models (teacher/class as random effects, addressing instructor_effect); learning gain (gain score) compared between groups. Task-learning separation: process_metrics are reported in a separate section explicitly labeled 'AI-present task performance' and never written into 'learning gain' conclusions (responding to task_vs_learning_guard and the E-002 lesson); learning_metrics use only no-AI independent assessment data. Risk analysis: between-group non-inferiority test of independent completion rate; illusion-of-competence difference (self-assessment − actual) between-group and over-time comparison; baseline-stratified heterogeneity analysis (E-005/E-009 differentiation tests). Compliance: control-group contamination check (self-report + anonymous questionnaire + computer-room spot checks), reporting both intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol analyses; report dropout rates and missing data (multiple imputation). Optional extension: add an unguardrailed group (standard AI interface) when resources allow, forming a three-arm design that replicates Bastani's 'unguardrailed -17% / guardrailed -0.004' policy contrast in the C context; transparent guardrail prompt-design process, validating guardrail replicability across ≥2 teacher classes.
evaluation.success_threshold: The introduction is judged net beneficial only when ALL of the following hold: (1) primary criterion — treatment group's end-of-term no-AI unified machine-based + written total is non-inferior to the control group (non-inferiority established, margin 0.3 SD; referencing Bastani E-002's unguardrailed -17% significant harm being eliminated under guardrails in E-003, the guardrail group must not show a same-magnitude negative effect); (2) learning gain (post-test − baseline) non-inferior to control; (3) risk indicators not significantly worse — no-AI independent task completion rate not below baseline and not significantly below control; illusion-of-competence difference (self-assessment − actual) not significantly larger than control; (4) retention and transfer tests not significantly worse than control; (5) AI usage frequency and learning gain not significantly negatively correlated (a significant negative correlation triggers a warning, even though the evidence set does not confirm a positive correlation, per the frame success_condition wording). Meeting these conditions yields generalizable introduction rules and accompanying instructional design; otherwise the allow policy is tightened or revoked.
stop_conditions: Week-8 no-AI mid-term independent quiz: treatment group significantly below control with effect size at Bastani's -17% magnitude (e.g., ≥0.2 SD or ≥10 percentage points) → immediately tighten guardrails or suspend the allow policy and assess causes

Two consecutive independent assessments (weeks 8 and 12) show the illusion-of-competence difference (self-assessment − actual) significantly widening with no improvement → strengthen metacognitive interventions, tighten usage scenarios if needed
No-AI independent completion rate drops below threshold (≥15 percentage points below baseline) or significantly below control → tighten the policy

Compliance breakdown: control-group AI usage too high (contamination rate ≥20% and uncontrollable) invalidating between-group comparison → stop between-group comparison or switch to observational analysis
Guardrail violations proliferate: share of homework directly submitting AI-generated code exceeds the preset cap (e.g., >30%) and does not decline within two weeks → suspend the allow policy

Differentiation breakdown: baseline-low groups' no-AI post-test relative performance significantly worsens (E-009 gap widening beyond preset tolerance) → implement differentiated restrictions or withdraw strugglers from the experiment
Academic-integrity incidents, tool failures, or policy implementation infeasibility prevent the intervention from running as designed → stop and document
